extracted.intended_audience: art historians, architects, sculptors, and students of architectural sculpture (particularly Venetian/renaissance funerary monuments)
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating funerary sculpture and tomb monuments
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging and understanding Venetian tomb sculpture (composition, iconography, workmanship, sentiment, and stylistic honesty) across Gothic, Byzantine-Renaissance, and Renaissance periods. Emphasises what makes a tomb effective or corrupt in taste, meaning, and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious feeling and heavenly hope
rubrics_metrics.description: Tombs should express religious humility and heavenly hope; the presence of religious imagery (Madonna, saints, legends) signals sincere devotional intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive examples: early tombs with Madonna enthroned, panels with saints and legends. Anti-pattern: monuments where religious means are limited (e.g., a single small Christ) and the rest is prideful display, indicating the vanishing of religious feeling in favor of state pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of the Virtues (theological/cardinal persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of the Virtues must be meaningful and truthful to the subject, not merely decorative or ironic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good when virtues relate to the person's character or public role (e.g., Justice, Temperance on Duccio's tomb). Bad when they are merely handsome, indistinguishable female figures recognized only by attributes, or used as public boast (virtues dressed as 'heathen goddesses' with no expression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of spiritual magnitudes in iconography
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptural composition should reflect the proper relation of God, angels, and man — Divine centrality and angelic subjection to the Divine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Christ enthroned with angels reverently looking to Him while human figures are subordinate. Avoid compositions that confuse spiritual relationships or place human ostentation above divine focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workmanship should serve sentiment, not replace it
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical excellence (chiselling, drawing, anatomy) is valuable only when it supports feeling and invention; pure skill without thought is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: Vendramin monument — exquisite chiselling but 'devoid of thought'; over-finish and mechanical precision used for vanity rather than emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid posture-making (grace at the cost of veracity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures should act and stand as they naturally would under the circumstances, not be contrived into graceful but unnatural poses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise for Giotto and Pre-Raphaelites for natural incident; criticism of later sculptors and painters who arrange attitudes primarily for beauty, producing lifelessness. In great hands posture can be noble, but with inferior practitioners it leads to lifeless composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful portraiture — represent the subject, not the carver
rubrics_metrics.description: Effigies should genuinely reflect the character of the deceased, not the carver's own mind or grotesque personal bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Foscari's effigy described as the carver's грусkly image rather than the Doge's true face; a noble portrait should not slander by inept or malign carving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and scale must be honest and appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural supports, columns, pedestals, and figure sizes must be in coherent proportion; not exaggerated to raise diminutive figures to prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: placing small Roman-armed figures on eleven-foot Corinthian shafts with multiple pedestals and brackets so the effect is pompous and absurd rather than noble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain the sarcophagus' character (avoid disguising the coffin)
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the sarcophagus ought not to be disguised into an elegant vase or mere pedestal; preserving its 'coffin' character is honest and appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical trend criticized: sarcophagus gradually losing four-square coffin form into refined vases and pedestals, turning the tomb into a stage for portraiture — a symptom of fear of death and pride of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shields and martial insignia should retain their functional honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Shields should look like practical war-gear, not merely decorative fields for armorial display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Renaissance shields shown repeatedly in ornate circular disks, surrounded by rays and gilding to look like ventilators or glory-ornaments, stripping them of soldierly reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iconographic honesty vs. classical display (avoid mere classical showmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute classical figures or Roman costume merely to display knowledge of classicism when it undermines religious or local meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: replacing angels with diminutive Roman-armored figures to show classical learning, where the substitution is merely ostentatious and strips religious content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning motive into ornament (curtains/tents vs. angels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motifs (like curtains introduced to accommodate angels) must not become dominant formal elements that obliterate the original devotional motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trend criticized: with Renaissance sculptors curtains/tents become huge and the angels merely pretexts for curtains; curtains growing into tent-beds and theatrical props is a degradation of intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence of style — avoid corrupt stylistic hybrids
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing incompatible stylistic elements (corrupt Gothic remnants with early Renaissance classicism) produces confused and degraded monuments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: tombs that are partly Gothic and partly classical, showing 'refuse of one style encumbering the embryo of another' and entangling principles of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous elaborate backgrounds and over-finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive background detail (landscapes, tricks of perspective, imitation of trees/clouds) and unnecessary under-cutting or over-finish in minor parts display vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good sculpture avoids mechanical display of skill in subordinate parts; technical show should not distract from primary effect on the spectator's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make allegorical figures expressive of their concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegorical personifications must display the character appropriate to their meaning (e.g., Fortitude should be resolute, not languid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Virtues reduced to 'handsome Venetian women' in courtly dress with little difference in expression; Fortitude leaning languidly and nearly toppling her column betrays mischaracterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid theatrical accumulation and grotesque spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Monuments should not become huge theatrical scenery with grotesque or theatrical elements that degrade taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: Pesaro monument with colossal grimacing caryatides, monsters, painted metal canopies, and stage-like portrait statues; such theatricality contradicts good sculptural taste and feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of civic pride and flattery overwhelming true memorial purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Tombs should not be primarily instruments of state pride, noble-family aggrandisement, or flattery expressed by allegory and inscriptions promising earthly/noble rewards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epitaphs and allegories that equate family nobility with angelic nobility or assert expected crowns from the judge are examples of classical/carnal pride to be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to simplicity can be a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: A simpler treatment and emphasis on public virtues (justice, peace, plenty) can be admirable and appropriate for civic tombs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Michael Steno's later-simple sarcophagus decorated only with simple crosses and an epitaph praising justice, peace, and plenty — valued for sincerity and civic-virtue focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture must have invention and feeling beyond mere imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: True merit involves invention and feeling; mere imitation of classical forms or slavish technical copying yields base and unworthy results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticises imitative English tomb-sculpture post-14th-century and Italian works that are 'perfect in workmanship and devoid of thought.' Seek originality and emotional truth rather than mechanical replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of pose relative to death (honest handling of mortality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitudes toward death in monuments should be honest: neither morbidly gruesome nor theatrically denying death by converting effigies into triumphant stage-actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trend criticized: semi-animate recumbent figures that 'rise up' or full-figured statues surrounded by Fame and Victory that pretend to bring resurrection down to earth — symptomatic of vanity and fear of death.
